items.followUp: State four uses of organic compounds in everyday life.

rubric.why: Award for identifying organic compounds as sources of essential everyday materials or energy.
rubric.description: Names uses such as food and fuels.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for at least two valid everyday uses, including food or fuel.

rubric.why: Award for identifying further useful products made from organic compounds.
rubric.description: Names useful products such as medicines, clothing or plastics.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for at least two valid products not already used for the first mark.

modelAnswer: Organic compounds are used as food and as fuels such as petrol and natural gas.
They are also used to make medicines, clothing fibres and plastics.

items.followUp: What is cracking of petroleum fractions? Name one product formed from naphtha by cracking.

rubric.why: Award for explaining what happens to the larger hydrocarbon molecules.
rubric.description: States that heating naphtha breaks larger hydrocarbon molecules into smaller ones.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the heating and breakdown into smaller hydrocarbons.

rubric.why: Award for naming a valid product of cracking.
rubric.description: Names a product such as petrol, an alkene or a hydrocarbon gas.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for at least one valid product.

modelAnswer: When naphtha is strongly heated, its larger hydrocarbon molecules break into smaller hydrocarbons; this process is called cracking.
The products include petrol and smaller hydrocarbons such as alkenes and gases.

items.followUp: Compare elements, compounds and mixtures by their composition and method of separation.

rubric.why: Award for distinguishing the basic composition of all three types of matter.
rubric.description: Identifies an element as one kind of atom, a compound as chemically combined elements, and a mixture as physically combined substances.
rubric.how: Give 2 marks when all three distinctions are stated; give 1 mark if two are correct.

rubric.why: Award for distinguishing the fixed composition of compounds from mixtures.
rubric.description: States that compounds have a fixed ratio of elements, whereas mixture components can be in any proportion.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for both parts of the comparison.

rubric.why: Award for comparing the properties of compounds and mixtures.
rubric.description: States that a compound has properties different from its constituent elements, while mixture components retain their properties.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for both parts of the comparison.

rubric.why: Award for distinguishing how compounds and mixtures can be separated.
rubric.description: States that compounds are separated chemically, while mixtures can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for both methods of separation.

modelAnswer: An element consists of only one kind of atom; a compound contains two or more elements chemically combined; a mixture contains substances physically mixed together.
The elements in a compound are present in a fixed proportion, whereas the components of a mixture may be present in any proportion.
A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements, while the components of a mixture retain their properties.
A compound can be separated into its elements by chemical means, whereas a mixture can be separated by physical methods.

items.followUp: State Bohr’s postulates about electron shells and the emission or absorption of energy.

rubric.why: Award for describing the atom's central structure.
rubric.description: States that the atom has a central nucleus with electrons around it.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for identifying both the nucleus and electrons.

rubric.why: Award for identifying the allowed paths or energy levels of electrons.
rubric.description: States that electrons move in fixed orbits or shells with definite energies.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for fixed orbits, shells or definite energy levels.

rubric.why: Award for the stability of electrons in permitted orbits.
rubric.description: States that electrons do not emit energy while in a permitted orbit.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for stating that electrons in stationary orbits do not radiate energy.

rubric.why: Award for explaining energy changes when an electron changes orbit.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs energy to move to a higher orbit and emits energy when it moves to a lower orbit.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for correctly describing either transition with its energy change.

modelAnswer: An atom has a small, positively charged nucleus at its centre, and electrons move around it.
Electrons can move only in certain fixed orbits, or shells, each having a definite energy.
An electron does not radiate energy while it remains in one of these permitted orbits.
An electron absorbs energy to move to a higher-energy orbit and emits energy when it falls to a lower-energy orbit.

items.followUp: Explain how a sodium atom forms an ionic bond with a chlorine atom, and how two hydrogen atoms form a covalent bond.

rubric.why: Award for identifying electron transfer in ionic bond formation.
rubric.description: States that sodium transfers an electron to chlorine.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the electron transfer from sodium.

rubric.why: Award for identifying the oppositely charged ions produced.
rubric.description: Shows that sodium and chlorine form Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for both ion charges.

rubric.why: Award for explaining the force that holds an ionic compound together.
rubric.description: States that electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions forms the ionic bond.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the attraction between the ions.

rubric.why: Award for identifying electron sharing as the basis of a covalent bond.
rubric.description: States that covalent bonding involves atoms sharing electrons.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for describing a shared electron pair.

rubric.why: Award for giving a valid covalent-bond example and its stable electron arrangement.
rubric.description: Explains that two hydrogen atoms share a pair of electrons to form H₂ and attain duplets.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the hydrogen example and shared-pair outcome.

modelAnswer: In sodium chloride, a sodium atom transfers one electron to a chlorine atom.
Sodium becomes Na⁺ and chlorine becomes Cl⁻.
The electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions forms an ionic bond.
In a covalent bond, atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
In H₂, each hydrogen atom contributes one electron to a shared pair, giving each atom a duplet.

items.followUp: According to Arrhenius, what ions do acids and bases produce in aqueous solution? Give one example of each.

rubric.why: Award for the Arrhenius definition of an acid.
rubric.description: States that an Arrhenius acid produces H⁺ ions in aqueous solution.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for both the ion and aqueous-solution condition.

rubric.why: Award for a correct acid example and its ionisation.
rubric.description: Gives HCl as an acid example producing H⁺ ions in water.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for a correct example and the acid ion.

rubric.why: Award for the Arrhenius definition of a base.
rubric.description: States that an Arrhenius base produces OH⁻ ions in aqueous solution.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for both the ion and aqueous-solution condition.

rubric.why: Award for a correct base example and its ionisation.
rubric.description: Gives NaOH as a base example producing OH⁻ ions in water.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for a correct example and the base ion.

modelAnswer: According to Arrhenius, an acid produces H⁺ ions when dissolved in water.
For example, HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).
An Arrhenius base produces OH⁻ ions when dissolved in water.
For example, NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).

items.followUp: Explain how atomic radius and ionization energy change from left to right across a period.

rubric.why: Award for stating the periodic trend in atomic radius.
rubric.description: States that atomic radius decreases across a period from left to right.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the correct direction of the trend.

rubric.why: Award for explaining the radius trend.
rubric.description: Explains that increasing nuclear charge attracts electrons in the same main shell more strongly.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for linking increasing nuclear charge and the same shell to the decrease in radius.

rubric.why: Award for stating the periodic trend in ionization energy.
rubric.description: States that ionization energy generally increases across a period from left to right.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the correct direction of the trend.

rubric.why: Award for explaining why electrons become more difficult to remove across a period.
rubric.description: Links the stronger nuclear attraction and smaller atomic radius to the greater energy needed to remove an electron.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the stronger attraction and 1 mark for its consequence: more energy is needed to remove the electron.

modelAnswer: Across a period from left to right, atomic radius decreases.
The nuclear charge increases while added electrons enter the same main shell, so the stronger attraction pulls the electron cloud closer to the nucleus.
Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
The outer electrons are held more strongly because of the increased nuclear attraction and smaller atomic radius, so more energy is needed to remove an electron.

items.followUp: Describe two harmful effects each of carbon monoxide and sulphur dioxide in air.

rubric.why: Award for a correct health effect of carbon monoxide.
rubric.description: States that carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin and reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying ability.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for linking carbon monoxide to haemoglobin or reduced oxygen transport.

rubric.why: Award for a correct harmful effect of sulphur dioxide.
rubric.description: States that sulphur dioxide harms the respiratory system or contributes to acid rain.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for one valid effect of sulphur dioxide.

rubric.why: Award for describing the harmful effects of other major air pollutants.
rubric.description: Names nitrogen oxides or particulate pollution and gives a valid effect, such as acid rain, smog or lung harm.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for a pollutant-effect pair.

rubric.why: Award for identifying another major pollutant and its environmental harm.
rubric.description: States that CFCs damage the ozone layer or that hydrocarbons contribute to photochemical smog.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for a correct pollutant-effect pair.

modelAnswer: Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin in the blood, reducing its ability to carry oxygen and causing serious health effects.
Sulphur dioxide irritates the respiratory system and can contribute to acid rain.
Nitrogen oxides can cause respiratory problems and contribute to acid rain and photochemical smog; particulate matter can damage the lungs.
Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) damage the ozone layer, while hydrocarbons can contribute to photochemical smog.
